newsitem.title: USA: NYNEX says to ease Internet phone jams.
newsitem.headline: NYNEX says to ease Internet phone jams.

text.p: NYNEX Corp is planning to introduce new technology to ease the strain of Internet traffic on its local phone network but the company still supports imposing controversial access charges on Internet users, an official said Wednesday.
"Internet growth is a challenge and an opportunity for us," Jeff Ward, NYNEX's vice president for policy, said in a telephone interview.
"We're designing a new product that will provide benefits to Internet access providers as well as to ourselves by taking Internet traffic essentially off the voice network," he said.
Ward declined to discuss the new system in detail, but said it would likely be introduced later this year.

A similiar product was announced by SBC Communications last week. Southwestern Bell will roll out the system to siphon off Internet traffic in its five-state regional phone network using equipment developed by Northern Telecom Ltd.
Like the SBC system, Ward said NYNEX will rely on a so-called packet-switching network to transmit Internet data.
Ordinary phone lines and switches make an unbroken connection when one party places a call to another.
That works efficiently for voice calls, but ties up the network needlessly when transmitting digital computer data which can be easily subdivided and sent in short bursts.

A packet-switching system would not maintain an unbroken connection between a consumer using the Internet and that consumer's Internet service provider, for example. Instead, the network opens a link only when data is sent or received.

Ward said the NYNEX packet system would operate between each local neighborhood phone switch and the rest of the phone system. A consumer would still place a call from home to the switch in the conventional manner.
Internet service providers could, however, link directly to the packet network, he said.

"That packet-based network will save the Internet provider money, because he won't have to buy a whole bank of modems, for example," Ward said. "And it will generate additional revenue for us because we can charge an appropriate amount for this extra service."

But NYNEX still believes that the Federal Communications Commission should allow local phone companies to charge an access fee on every call to Internet service providers, like the fees charged on calls to long distance firms, Ward said.

"There are two generic solutions we're addressing," Ward explained. "One is a regulatory driven solution that would have access fees, a successor to access fees or something like access fees paid by Internet service providers."
"Another piece of it is to reengineer the network to meet the emerging needs of customers who are heavy Internet service providers," he said. "We're pursuing both ways."

Ward said he was reluctant to enter the debate over the effect of Internet use on the phone network. Some local phone comapnies have argued that Internet use is threatening to overwhelm the system, justifying access fees for new equipment.
But earlier on Wednesday, a group of Internet and computer companies released a study that they said refuted the phone company claims.

"NYNEX is not one of these companies going around saying 'the sky is falling, the sky is falling' on Internet use," Ward said. "Anytime we're selling more of our service, that is a good thing, not a bad thing."
He did criticize Internet companies' common practice of charging a flat rate for unlimited monthly access.

"No long distance company in the world charges in that fashion and it creates an uneconomic price," Ward said. "The result of that price is heavy users -- Internet users tend to be heavy users -- are getting quite a bargain."
--Aaron Pressman((202-898-8312))
